title: Conscription as an element in European Union preparedness
text:
### BRIEFING

Author: Eleni Lazarou with Panagiotis Politis Lamprou Members' Research Service PE 769.541 – March 2025 EN

## Conscription as an element in

## European Union preparedness

SUMMARY

Once considered an issue of the past, conscription has increasingly made its way back onto 
European, EU and global policy agendas in recent years, mainly since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 
2022. As EU defence policy has steadily progressed,with new procurement initiatives and defence 
industry reinforcement, a parallel discussion on the EU's armed forces is evolving in the context of 
the EU's common security and defence policy (CSDP). Europe's civilian and military preparedness 
and readiness has also come under the spotlight recently, as highlighted by the report presented in 
October 2024 by former Finnish President Sauli Niinistö. Opinion polls in some Member States also 
show growing support for the reintroduction of national service or conscription. Mounting threats to 
European security, fears of transatlantic disengagement, as well as the position of the new United 
States administration and potential peace plans for Ukraine involving the presence of European 
troops, has raised awareness of the need to ready Member States' armed forces for the most 
extreme military contingencies. 
The conscription landscape across the EU is diverse. National defence is primarily carried out by 
professional armed forces, but conscription is becoming increasingly relevant. Some EU countries 
retained conscription practices beyond the end of the Cold War, while others reintroduced 
conscription modalities following Russia's 2022 invasion. Peacetime conscription policies differ 
among Member States in, among other things, the number of conscripts, the length of service, the 
level of compensation provided, and the size of the reserve forces.The Niinistö report underscored 
the potential importance of conscription in developing a holistic 'total defence' concept that 
connects military and civil defence, while promoting a 'whole-of-society' approach to crisis response 
and preparedness. It also proposes increasing structured exchanges between Member States to 
identify national service and conscription model best practices, potentially facilitated by the EU. 
Some experts have highlighted the benefits of implementing conscription, while others are sceptical 
of poorly trained and ill-equipped conscript armies. The European Parliament has repeatedly 
underlined the limited number of personnel devoted to CSDP missions and operations, highlighting 
issues related to force generation.

• Background 
• Conscription systems in the EU 
• Conscription, total defence and preparedness 
• European Parliament position 

#### Background

Conscription has long been a defining feature of defence policies in Europe, shaping national security and defence strategies for centuries.By definition, conscription(or the 'draft') refers to an obligatory enrolment for service in a country's armed forces. Duration, eligibility, exemption and alternative service options vary between different states. While some EU Member States have abolished or suspended their conscription systems since the end of the Cold War, others continue to rely on this integral part of their military readiness. The debate surrounding conscription has inevitably resurfaced due to the deteriorating international security situation. Nevertheless, conscription remains a national competence at the core of state sovereignty. As such, discussions for the time being revolve around national (not supranational/EU) conscription. At the same time, most EU Member States continue to rely on their professional armed forces, but may look to conscription in the pursuit of additional human resources and enhanced military readiness. As an overall trend, European armed forces were in significant decline in the decade preceding the onset of Russia's war on Ukraine. In 2020, a report by the European Organisation of Military Associations and Trade Unions (EUROMIL) highlighted that, of the 15 European (including non-EU) countries it had surveyed, over two thirds 'decreased the personnel strength of their military in the period between 2010 and 2020. The actual number of personnel serving decreased on average by 16 %; 26.5 % in Belgium and 25 % in Germany are the largest decreases, while Slovakia (7 %) and Greece (5 %) are on the lower end of the scale'. A growing threat environment in the past decade and, above all, Russia's war against Ukraine, has steadily rekindled interest in reviving conscription and reserve forces, globally and in EU countries. In March2024, the President of Latvia, EdgarsRinkēvičs, stated that, despite conscription's unpopularity, 'armed forces across Europe faced recruitment difficulties and conscription would help build up more capable reserve forces to deter Russia' and that 'there is a need for serious discussion about conscription'. More recently, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared in March2025 that Poland will 'try to have a model ready by the end of this year so that every adult male … is trained in the event of war'. In February 2025, the Belgian Defence Minister shared plans to send letters to all 18-year-olds, inviting them to participate in voluntary military service. Germany'sDefence Minister declaredin late 2023 that the suspension of compulsory military service 'was a mistake'. Ukraine, now entering a fourth year of war, lowered its minimum conscription age from 27 to 25 years in April 2024, after having reinstated conscription in 2014 due to the security situation in eastern Ukraine. In November 2024, the US reportedly pressed Ukraine to lower its military recruitment age to 18to address manpower shortages. The trend also applies to non-like minded countries, such as Russia, which tries to replenish its troops through conscripts, convicts and 'imported' troops from North Korea. China adopted new conscription rules in 2023, which aim to address human resource issues (e.g. former soldiers can now be mobilised 'as a supplement to active service units'), suggesting that 'it continues to suffer from poor retention of its personnel'. Concern and debate about the size of European armed forces has accentuated since the inauguration of the second Trump administration. In the context of its approach to the future of Ukraine, and a possible ceasefire deal between Russia and Ukraine, the new administration has reiterated its position that European armed forces should take on the task of providing security guarantees. As reported in February 2025, the US asked European capitals to provide 'detailed proposals on the weaponry, peacekeeping troops (specific numbers of troop brigades they would be prepared to deploy) and security arrangements they could provide Ukraine with as part of any security guarantees to end its war with Russia'. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization's Secretary General, Mark Rutte, has also raised the need for Europe to prepare for war on multiple occasions, most recently in the 2025 Munich Security Conference. Experts also cite concerns about potential US force withdrawals from Europe, which would require European forces to replace them. It is estimated that, in an 'effective US withdrawal' scenario, 'an increase in European capacities

equivalent to the fighting capacity of 300 000 US troops is needed' – roughly 50 new European 
brigades.Both 'Trump and Putin are causing a rethink' of conscriptionpolicies. 
As exemplified by manpower shortages in Russia and Ukraine, recruitment is a crucial policy issue 
for modern armed forces, not least for EU countries which have traditionally encountered 
recruitment challenges and are now faced with a dramatically changed geopolitical landscape. As 
Europeans recognise the need to 'turn the EU's geopolitical awakening into a more permanent 
strategic posture', maintaining a strong and sustainable military force is important. Consequently, 
this strategic environment has reignited discussionon whether conscription should be reconsidered 
as a solution to address manpower shortages. In the meantime, the need to be prepared for 'the 
most extreme military contingencies', in the words of Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, 
requires that EU Member States improve their forces' combat readiness. 
Even before February 2022, a number of experts had identified the challenges associated with the 
process of obtaining troop contributions ('force generation'), highlighting that the Union faces 
unpredictability and resource shortfalls, particularly regarding availability. Under the 'Act' chapter, 
the Strategic Compass (a 2022 actionable framework for the EU's security and defence to 2030, 
containing 81 deliverables), refers to the need to incentivise force generation for military missions 
and operations by 'enhancing transparency and predictability in the rotation of troops' and 
'expanding the scope of common costs under the European Peace Facility'. Force generation for 
military operations requires that the Member States agree on their contributions and then allocate 
personnel to pre-established positions with predefined ranks and qualifications. Force generation 
will be particularly crucial for the EU's rapid deployment capacity, a Compass deliverable,to ensure 
that personnel and assets (e.g., strategic enablers) are available for rapid deployment. The allocation 
of responsibilities for determining the number of military personnel varies: in some Member States, 
government takes the decision on numbers; while in others, the government and the parliament 
share the decision. In five countries identified in the EUROMIL report, the decision lies with the 
parliament. 
The October 2024 Niinistö Report on strengthening Europe's civilian and military preparedness and 
readiness alluded to the potential relevance of military conscriptionto establishing a total defence 
concept, linking military and civil defence,and in promoting a whole-of-society approach to crises 
and preparedness. More specifically, the former Finnish President and current special adviser to the 
President of the European Commission proposed to establish structured exchanges between 
Member States 'to identify best practices in relation to national service and conscription models'. 
Additionally, Niinistö called for the EU to 'build on and complement ongoing discussions and 
initiatives on national service and conscription models' as part of a collective effort tomake careers 
in defence, security and emergency response more attractive toyounger generations. Furthermore, 
the report made reference to recent opinion polls in Belgium, France, Germany, Lithuania and the 
Netherlands, whose results indicate growing public support for the reintroduction of national service 
or conscription.Discussions about the promotion of a whole-of-society and total defence approach, 
potentially including the participation of younger generations in the security and defence sectors, 
may also be relevant to the upcoming EU preparedness union strategy, included in the 2025 
Commission work programme. 
Military conscription is also debated in the NATO context. In 2023, the then Chair of the NATO 
Military Committee stated that Finland had built an effective military and reserve through its 
conscription system. Similarly, in 2023 a former British defence secretary praised Finnish and 
Swedish (reserve) models, noting 'conscription and reserve(s) often go hand in hand'. Experts 
indicate that NATO does not have enough troops to execute the military plans already agreed upon. 
For example, the Allies need to address their personnel shortfalls (among other shortcomings) in 
order to ensure that the obligations under NATO's New Force Model (i.e. the large pool of high 
readiness forces based on different force tiers) are met.In the context of new transatlantic relations
